trans.sense: to frighten or cause hesitation; to daunt, put off; to disconcert, perturb

examples.text: Jumping out of an airplane does not faze him, yet he is afraid to ride a roller coaster.
But we're / Not getting anywhere. Nothing / fazes her.
examples.ref: 1965, Catullus, translated by Barriss Mills, The Carmina of Catullus: A Verse Translation, [West Lafayette, Ind.]: Purdue University Studies, →OCLC, carminum 42, page 71:

examples.text: In the dreary world / That we're living in / It's fashionable / To let nothing faze you
examples.ref: 1978, “Living in a Dream”, in On the Edge, performed by Sea Level:

examples.text: Some individuals "can't hold their liquor" and become thoroughly intoxicated on small amounts of alcohol which would not faze most social drinkers.
examples.ref: 1990, “Assessment”, in Broadening the Base of Treatment for Alcohol Problems: Report of a Study by a Committee of the Institute of Medicine, Division of Mental Health and Behavioral Medicine, Washington, D.C.: National Academy Press, →ISBN, section III (Aspects of Treatment), pages 252–253:

examples.text: He sticks it out even further in the scherzo, fazing the listener with displaced accents, and then inserting a malicious pause just when we seem to have found our feet.
examples.ref: 2009, Richard Wigmore, The Faber Pocket Guide to Haydn, London: Faber and Faber, →ISBN, page 192:

examples.text: [Gareth] Southgate should be absolutely clear now that [Jordan] Pickford is not fazed by the big occasion but, on the flip-side, he might not be too thrilled his goalkeeper was involved so much.
